caption:
It honestly feels surreal to finally be saying this... Five years later and we’re officially breaking ground on our forever home!

When we bought this farm, we imagined it to be a place where our family could spend quality time together, be outdoors, and build a home that we could grow old in.

We jumped into designing right away, and we actually designed the entire house! But eventually, we realized the house we were planning just didn’t feel right. So we hit pause.

Then life happened. Changes in our family lives, businesses, and the property itself took priority. And the house build plans took a back seat. The dream wasn’t over, but what happened next made it feel like our dream was getting further and further away...

The 2023 Kelowna wildfires changed everything. Watching so much of the farm burn was heartbreaking, and for a while, we weren’t sure this dream would ever become a reality. We were so grateful that our little farmhouse survived the fires, because so many people in our community weren’t so lucky...

But over time, as Justin poured countless hours into restoring the property, I felt like our dream maybe wasn’t so far away.

Celebrating one of the happiest days of our lives by getting married right here on the farm under the willow tree felt very full circle.

Starting over gave us a chance to design a home that truly reflects who we are and what our family needs.

I feel like we are creating a place where our family can make memories for years to come, and we can’t wait to bring you along for the ride.

Next up... I’m going to give you a sneak peek at the design process. I’m so thrilled with how it’s coming together. Stay tuned for more!

We’ve held onto this one for a few days, wanting to give Matt the space to grieve before we put it into words. But Milo deserves to be celebrated, so here we are. Last week, my brother said goodbye to Milo. If you knew Milo, you knew he wasn’t just a dog. He was family.

He came into our lives when we were still kids, grew up alongside our dog Mario, and just never stopped showing up. 17 years. He was Matt’s ride or die in every sense of the word. He travelled the world with him, seen more places from a little suitcase than most people ever will. He was there for the big moments too, including the day I proposed to my wife Jillian. He just took it all in stride, because that was Milo.

He was Nacho’s first best friend. His hero. His savior. And when we lost Nacho almost a year ago, Milo kept going. He met every new animal, every new family member, and carried that love forward a little longer than the rest of us got to. We like to think they’re together again now. Reunited on the other side of the rainbow bridge, Nacho finally getting to thank him in person.

No matter how much time you get, nothing prepares you for losing your best friend. Our hearts are a little heavier, and they will be for a while. 17 incredible years, Milo. You were deeply loved, and you’ll be deeply missed.

I got married. A couple of the boys met their soulmates. Others have babies on the way. Some made massive changes in their lives, financially, personally, in business, investing, growing into the next version of themselves.

Am I saying you need to go to Nimmo Bay to experience this? Absolutely not. But I do think there’s something really powerful about slowing down and truly connecting with your people. That kind of time together matters more than we realize.

Part 1/2! It’s crazy to think it’s almost been a year since I had the most epic bachelor party ever. Looking back on this trip now, I’m honestly so glad we did it this way.

Maybe it was being at Nimmo Bay. Maybe it was unplugging for a few days. But I think the biggest thing was just spending real quality time with your people.

No distractions. No noise. Just 6 buddies who’ve known each other since we were kids, hanging out, connecting, laughing until it hurt, having real conversations, being vulnerable, and somehow all leaving better versions of ourselves.

caption:
Another packed weekend, started where it always does, out at the farm. The irrigation isn’t fully finished, we’re still dialing in the automation and a few smaller details, but the big win is I’m officially done hand watering 500 trees one at a time like it’s 1850. Huge relief. And having all 500 English oaks actually in the ground still doesn’t feel real some days.

Then there’s the birdhouse situation, which has become a bigger project than I ever expected, but building these out across the orchard feels like one of those things that actually matters, so I’m not complaining.

My brother came down and we celebrated my dad’s 65th, Kelowna edition, which meant a stop at the Kelowna Bocce Club, obviously. The food was incredible, the butcher especially, good enough that I’m now seriously scheming about putting a bocce lane on the property myself. We got way too competitive for a casual afternoon and it might be the hardest I’ve laughed in months.

There’s no photo of it, but my nono played at that same club when he first immigrated from Italy, and years later made it to the BC Summer Games for bocce. Standing in that same spot with my dad and my brother hit different.

Sunday was family, my brother and Maude in from the island, just soaking up a genuinely great weekend before the biggest update of all.

Foundation’s up. Concrete’s pouring today. Talked about this house for so long it stopped feeling real, and now it’s happening. Taking you guys along for this one. Lot more coming.

caption:
We finally got the trees in. Three years. Let that sink in. 😉

This whole thing started with my neighbor. He helped me out when I wrecked my ankle, and somewhere in there he planted a different kind of seed and introduced me to the idea of truffles. I had no clue it would turn into this.

Three years later, here we are. Multiple trips to truffle conventions. Studying, learning, planning, prepping. Import licensing. Irrigation design. Row spacing. Equipment. Figuring out which truffle type even makes sense for this land. You name it, I went down the rabbit hole on it. Three years of that to get 500 trees in the ground. Not bad for a city boy with zero farming experience, unless you count the flower farming that apparently turned me into a farmer somewhere along the way.

Now for the fun part. I masterminded my airport duty and sent @mattaugust to grab @elliot.j.berenger and boat him across the lake. A proper welcome to Kelowna. Then Elliot’s flight got delayed two hours, and by the time Matt dropped him off the lake had turned into a full storm. So Elliot got the scenic arrival, and Matt got to fight his way back across it solo. Pretty sure I know who came out worse on that one. And that was just the start. Pretty sure Elliot was picturing a relaxing weekend away. Instead I handed him a fistful of bamboo stakes and grow tubes and put him to work around the new saplings. And we nailed it. Like the rugby team we used to be, we took the field of trees and cleared all 500.

After a brutal day, the boys took over dinner. I got fully influenced into buying these spanish sardines, so we built a little spread around them, tested out the new cheese from @cows_creamery, threw in a salad straight from the garden, and opened a bottle of wine. Okay, two. Sunday was all about Matt and @adria.august and their gender reveal. It’s a girl!! Could not be happier for them.  Of course Matt pulls out the helicopter! True Matty style. 

Can’t wait to meet the newest little member of the crew. Annie is Pumped! Good friends, three years in the making, and a reminder that summer is basically knocking on the door. Epic weekend.

caption:
Still mentally in Japan… and honestly not sure I’ve come all the way back yet.

Somewhere between the quiet mornings, the rhythm of the trains, and the way everything just flows over there, something sticks with you. I caught myself a few days after getting home instinctively bowing to people instead of saying thanks… like my brain hadn’t quite switched back to Canadian settings.

There’s a different pace there. A respect for the little things. The way a simple meal, a walk down a side street, even grabbing a coffee feels more intentional. You don’t fully notice it while you’re in it… but the second you leave, you feel it.

We were there for almost three weeks, which is a long time by most standards… and somehow it still felt like we were just scratching the surface. Not in a “we missed things” way, but in a “we barely got to live it” kind of way.

Also… somehow feel like I didn’t eat enough ramen. The scale back home would strongly disagree with that take.

Trip of a lifetime, no question.
Now it just feels like we need to go back… and do it a little slower next time.

caption:
We’re back in the kitchen with a delicious savoury breakfast meal. Italian style, of course. Eggs in Purgatory. One of Jill’s all-time favourites… although her version is usually tomato sauce + eggs in the microwave. We’re making this the right way today.

Recipe below! 👇

Ingredients
1/2 onion, finely chopped
1 clove garlic, minced
12 oz crushed tomatoes
4 eggs
Fresh Basil
Oregano q.b.
Salt & Pepper q.b.
Olive Oil

Recipe:
Heat olive oil in a medium skillet over medium heat.
Add the finely chopped onion and sauté for 3-4 minutes, or until translucent.
Add the minced garlic and cook for an additional minute, stirring constantly to prevent burning.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and add the basil, oregano, salt, and pepper to taste. Stir well.
Lower the heat and let the sauce simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Using a spoon, create four small wells in the sauce.
Crack one egg into each well.
Cover the skillet with a lid and cook for 4-5 minutes, or until the egg whites are set but the yolks remain runny (or to your desired doneness).
Remove from heat and garnish with additional basil.
Serve hot with crusty bread for dipping

caption:
Interrupting Japan content momentarily to share this incredible recipe I made before we left! This one brought back a funny memory! Today I’m making Pizzocheri, a traditional dish from the northern Alps of Italy in Valtellina… and here’s the wild part. I actually passed through that exact valley on my way to the Junior Worlds in Valmalenco. That was 18 years ago today. 

This dish is about as mountain-comfort-food as it gets: cabbage, potatoes, buckwheat pasta… lots of cheese… and of course garlic. And yes, I finished it with a drizzle of olive oil because it wouldn’t be a Justin Pasutto recipe if I didn’t sneak a little olive oil on top. You knew it was coming.

Ingredients:
1 pound Yukon Gold potatoes (3 medium)
1 pound savoy cabbage
1 garlic clove
8 ounces Alpine-style cow’s milk cheese (Valtellina Casera, fontina, Kaltbach Le Crémeux or young Gruyère)
8 ounces Grana Padano or Parmesan
3 cups plus 1 tablespoon / 400 g buckwheat flour, plus more for dusting
¾ cup / 100 g “Tipo 00” flour or all-purpose flour
1¼ cups warm water, plus more if needed
Kosher salt
12 tablespoons / 170 g unsalted butter (preferably European-style)
Freshly ground black pepper

Recipe:
Start the vegetables: Peel the potatoes and cut them into 1-inch pieces. Cut out the core from the cabbage and tear the leaves into large chunks. Thinly slice the garlic. Set a large pot of water to boil.

Prep the cheeses: Remove any rind from the Alpine-style cheese and slice thinly. Finely grate the Grana Padano and toss both cheeses together.

Make the pasta: Mix the two flours together, form a mound with a well in the center, add warm water, and stir to form a shaggy dough. Knead until soft and pliable.

Roll the dough 2–3 mm thick, cut into sheets, then slice into short ribbons.

Salt the boiling water. Cook potatoes for 2 minutes, add cabbage, bring back to a boil, then add pasta. Cook 10–13 minutes until tender.

Meanwhile melt butter with garlic over medium-low heat until golden and fragrant.

Layer pasta and vegetables with cheese in the warmed baking dish.

Finish with the garlic butter so the cheese melts into a rich, fondue-like sauce.

Serve immediately with freshly ground black pepper.

Last stop… Okinawa.

I know Jill and I shared a post together on this part of the trip, but I wanted to put something down from my side too.

We came here for one reason, longevity. A true blue zone, or at least part of the island is known as one. We expected a Japanese version of Hawaii, beaches, culture, slower pace of life.

But what we found was something completely different.

At first glance, it’s not what you think. More concrete, less of that traditional Japan feel. But once you start to understand the history, war, devastation, and a 27 year American occupation, it starts to make sense. And it hits you pretty hard.

What stood out most though was the culture underneath it all.

The food alone tells a story. Sanpin cha tea everywhere, I brought a ton home. Okinawan purple sweet potato worked into everything from breakfast to desserts. Simple ingredients tied to longevity. The pottery, the small details, the quiet pride, it’s all there if you slow down enough to see it.

We definitely didn’t have enough time to fully experience it, and I’d go back in a heartbeat.

If you’re coming here, don’t judge it too quickly. It might not look like the tropical paradise you had in your head, but once you start peeling back the layers, you realize Okinawa has something way deeper to offer.

Grateful we came without really knowing what to expect and left with a whole new perspective.

caption:
Jill and I flew into Calgary this past weekend to shop for windows for the new house. For those that have been following along, we’ve officially started building out at the farm… about five years after buying it. We definitely thought we’d be living there by now, but between taking our time, COVID, the fires, life, weddings, and Jill’s mom getting sick, there were a few curveballs along the way.

But we’re finally here.

Right now we’re in that phase of actually getting our hands on everything, touring different companies, not to promote them, but to really see and feel the product and make sure we’re choosing the right pieces. This one’s special to us. We’re building it with the intention that it’s our forever home.

What started as a quick trip turned into a full tour. They went above and beyond and spoiled us with lunch… and those Jilly Box macarons didn’t stand a chance.

I stretched the trip a bit so I could sneak in an appointment with Dr. Salami. He’s been a staple in this ankle recovery. Truly nobody does it like him. While I was there I caught a Calgary Flames game too. Battle of Alberta still alive and well. Jill told me not to come home.

caption:
After 4 days in Tokyo and 2 days at Disney we were cooked 😂 like full system overload, so we packed it up and headed to Hakone and this was a trip within the trip. 

Train to Odawara then more trains and then onto this wild mountain train that literally crawls its way up the hill on an 8% grade, steepest in Japan and second steepest in the world, with switchbacks and slow climbs and the kids glued to the windows, honestly one of the coolest parts of the whole journey. And then you arrive and everything just shifts, misty mountain air, dead quiet, tucked up about 500m above everything and you can actually feel your body exhale. 

We stayed at Gora Kadan and went all in on the traditional ryokan experience, something my brother Matt told us was a non negotiable and he was bang on, kimonos, tatami mats, sleeping on the floor which the kids thought was the greatest thing ever, and these insane multi course meals brought right to the room, like next level. And the onsens, natural hot springs, yeah fully naked , separated by gender and different from home but once you lean into it, it is actually unreal. 

This place slowed everything down, it reset our whole nervous system in a way I did not even realize we needed. If you are planning a Japan trip do not skip the traditional ryokan , it is not just a stop it is a reset button, trust me.

caption:
First 24hrs in Japan 🇯🇵 and honestly… I can’t explain it.

There’s 38 million people in this city, but what hits you right away isn’t the size, it’s the respect. The cleanliness. The way people carry themselves and take pride in where they live. It’s next level. There are so many epic things here, but the fact that what feels like 90% of people genuinely care about their environment… it’s seriously impressive.

Immediate culture shock.

We hit Tokyo Tower, Zojo-ji temple, then took on the train system which is an unbelievable experience in itself. Clean, quiet, insanely efficient… even each station has its own jingle which just adds to the whole vibe.

Made our way to Shibuya Crossing and walked the world’s largest crosswalk, organized chaos at its finest. Then Takeshita Street, which feels like the exact place you go when you “gotta go” 😂 absolute madness, but we had a good laugh.

Slowed it down at Meiji Shrine and the sake barrel wall. Walking through that park into the temple… there’s just a feeling there. Hard to explain but it hits.

Topped it off with some proper Takumi style ramen and called it.

Jet lag is real, we’re up way too early, but the kids are absolute legends. They’re so fired up to be here and taking it all in.

And we’re just getting started.

You can feel the history here. Like the nature is unreal, but some of the architecture feels heavy and a bit worn. Not bad… just different. And kind of emotional if you really sit with it, the more you learn. 

We kept saying over and over… 3 days was NOT enough.

We didn’t snorkel. Didn’t make it down to the south end. Didn’t even come close to doing everything we wanted. But I truly feel like it ended up being exactly what we needed. A place to slow down, reset, let the kids just be, and wrap up THE most epic family trip.

My mom raised my brother and me with a lot of love, but also a very clear understanding of right and wrong. She held our family together and cared deeply about our education, our faith, how we treated people, and what kind of men we were becoming. 

And like most good moms… when she was proud of us, it meant everything. When she was mad… we knew we were in serious trouble. Looking back now as a parent myself, I realize just how much of the foundation of who I am came from her. I’m far from perfect, but the values of family, loyalty, and showing up for the people you love were built early and they came from her. Everything we’re building today started with women like them. And now Annie’s watching it all unfold. Being a girl dad changes you. It makes you realize that being the right kind of man really matters, because she’s learning what to look for by watching me. 

Today I’m grateful for the women who raised me, the woman I get to stand beside, and the young women who’s watching it all. Happy International Women’s Day.

This was supposed to be a routine follow-up trip to Calgary.

Two years ago, a retired orthopedic surgeon who became a neighbour — and then a friend — told me, “If you want your life back, go see this guy.” So I waited. Two years for the consult. Worth every single day. Huge thanks to him, because I never would have found this path without that nudge.

But I also learned something important along the way: in Canada, healthcare is free… but no one is actually advocating for you except you. Before I ever changed direction, I did everything that was asked of me. More X-rays. More scans. Injections. Physio. Rehab. I put in the work exactly as prescribed. Not to “prove anyone wrong” — but to build a real case that what I was doing wasn’t working and that I needed something different.

I had to go get my records. I had to collect my reports. I even found another specialist in Vancouver to compare opinions and make sure I was choosing the right path. It wasn’t fast. It wasn’t simple. But it was worth it.

This week was about full X-rays, full checkups, honest conversations, and setting a real baseline for physio back home. And the part that still blows my mind: for the first time in 5 years, I’m walking without pain. And somehow… I’m 3 weeks ahead of schedule. Dr. Jeremy and the team at @talarismedical gave me my life back — but I had to go find them first.

If you’re dealing with a foot or ankle issue, comment “ANKLE” and I’ll send you what I learned about how to navigate the system and advocate for yourself. Rehab phase starts now. Kelowna, let’s get to work!

caption:
Holiday parties are coming… and let’s be honest... who actually has time for complicated recipes?  I’m all about easy, tasty, crowd-pleasing snacks so here’s this holiday crostini with a twist. 

I swapped out the pear slices for crushed walnuts, making it totally customizable. Perfect for last-minute hosting—or just keeping your snack game strong! 

You’re gonna wanna save this one, because your guests (and your sanity) will thank you.

Ingredients: 
- 1 baguette
- olive oil
- 1 1/2 cup ricotta cheese
- pinch of salt
- crushed walnuts
- prosciutto 
- hot honey
- pomegranate seeds
- fresh rosemary

 Slice your baguette and brush olive oil on each piece. Place on a lined baking sheet and bake at 350°F for 5–10 minutes, until crispy.

Make the whipped ricotta spread. Add ricotta, olive oil, and salt to a food processor or blender. Blend for 30 seconds to 1 minute, until completely smooth.

Prepare the topping: Place the whipped ricotta, prosciutto, crushed walnuts, and a generous drizzle of hot honey on a cutting board or in a bowl. Chop or mix everything together, then transfer to a serving dish. Finish with more hot honey, freshly cracked black pepper, fresh rosemary, pomegranate seeds, and a pinch of salt.

Dip your crostinis, scoop, and enjoy!

caption:
I didn’t set out to do a 40-hour fast... It was supposed to be 36 but life happened. Kids needed to get to school, the day kept moving, and before I knew it… 40 hours had passed.

Ever since my surgery, I’ve had this pull to do a longer water fast. I did a 24-hour one earlier this summer and honestly, it felt incredible. 

I’ve been focused on reducing overall inflammation and starting the new year with a clean slate. When you fast, your body enters a process called autophagy—basically your cells taking out the trash and repairs themselves. That process really starts to kick in around 24 hours and gets more robust the longer you go.

So I figured… if I’m doing this, why not go all in? Not gonna lie... it wasn’t easy. There were moments where food sounded very convincing. But there was also something powerful about slowing down and letting my body do what it’s designed to do.

This isn’t health advice, and fasting isn’t for everyone. If you’re curious, talk to your doctor and see if it’s something that makes sense for you. All I’ll say is this: sometimes the reset you need isn’t another plan, program, or purchase. Sometimes it’s just giving your body a minute to catch up.

And yeah… drink responsibly. 💧😉

caption:
Headed to the Blue Zone for this one… Sardinia, Italy to be exact 🇮🇹 I’ve been diving into @danbuettner cookbooks for a while now... packed with stories, lifestyle tips, and insanely delicious recipes, so I decided to bring a little Sardinian magic into the kitchen.

Cooking these recipes feels like a little trip to Sardinia without leaving the house. I started by prepping the flatbread, and while that was resting, I got the minestrone going. Perfect cozy dinner for these colder months! Recipe below👇 

🥖 Sardinia Flatbread
• 1 ½ cups all-purpose flour
• 1 ½ cups semolina flour
• 1 ½ cups warm water
• 1 packet (¼ oz) active dry yeast
• Pinch of salt
• Olive oil & sea salt for serving

Mix flours, water, yeast, and salt.
Divide dough into quarters (or smaller pieces) and let rest 1 hr.
Preheat oven 375°F. Roll dough paper-thin.
Bake 2 mins per side on a lightly oiled pan.
Brush with olive oil & sprinkle with sea salt to serve.

🍲 Sardinia Minestrone
• ½ cup dried fava beans (or canned lima beans)
• ½ cup dried cranberry beans (or canned Romano beans)
• ⅓ cup dried chickpeas (or canned chickpeas)
• 7 tbsp olive oil
• 1 medium onion, chopped
• 2 medium carrots, chopped
• 2 celery stalks, chopped
• 2 tsp minced garlic
• 1 (28-oz) can crushed tomatoes
• 3 medium potatoes, diced
• 1 ½ cups chopped fennel
• ¼ cup parsley, chopped
• 2 tbsp basil, chopped
• ⅔ cup fregula, Israeli couscous, or acini di pepe
• ½ tsp salt & ½ tsp pepper
• ¼ cup grated pecorino Romano

(Optional) Soak dried beans overnight; I used canned.
Heat 3 tbsp olive oil in a pot. Cook onion, carrots, celery until soft (~5 min). Add garlic 20 sec.
Stir in tomatoes, potatoes, fennel, parsley, basil, and beans. Add water to cover by 1 inch.
Bring to boil, then simmer 1.5 hrs until beans tender. Add water if needed.
Stir in pasta, salt & pepper. Simmer 10 min until pasta tender.
